newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya steps up moves to free kidnapped Britons.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya steps up moves to free kidnapped Britons.

text.p: Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov on Sunday lambasted his top security officials over the kidnap of two Britons and gave them 24 hours to come up with a plan to free them and other hostages.

Chechnya's Prosecutor-General Khalash Serbiyev told the meeting that hostage-taking was becoming a huge problem in the republic, where Russian troops fought a bloody campaign against separatist forces for 21 months until last August.
At least 32 people are in detention on kidnapping charges, Radio Russia quoted Serbiyev as saying.
Abductions have occurred on a regular basis since hostilities ended in the breakaway republic, and its leaders, who humiliated the Russian army during the conflict, have been unable to stop them.

"Maskhadov sharply criticised the leaders of the security ministries and ordered them to present him with a detailed plan of measures to free people taken hostage," Deputy President Vakha Arsanov told Interfax news agency.
Chechen police said earlier a special group had been set up to search for the two British aid workers, grabbed from the house where they were staying by a group of armed, masked men.
British officials said on Saturday the two, Camilla Carr and Jon James, were abducted on Wednesday night. Chechen officials had said earlier that they had been taken on Thursday night.
Hostage-takers usually ask for money for the return of their captors but by Sunday there had been no word of any demands for the release of the Britons, whose whereabouts were unknown.
Both Russian and Chechen authorities said the two had failed to report their presence in the volatile region.

But an official from the local prosecutor's office said the Centre for Peacemaking and Community Development where they worked had been registered in Chechnya on December 22, 1996 by Briton Christopher Hunter.
The centre was involved in the psychological rehabilitation of children affected by the conflict, in which tens of thousands of people died and many more were injured or made homeless.
A representative of the Centre, Olga Pavlova, said Hunter had met Chechen Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov last month.

Interfax said Pavlova, speaking from the southern Russian town of Stavropol from where she was due to travel to Chechnya on Monday, also defended the centre's deputy director Adnan Adayev, who was arrested by police on Saturday morning.
The couple's two bodyguards were also detained.

"Adayev and three of his comrades always ensured our safety over several months which were full of attempts to get in the way of the Centre's work," the agency quoted Pavlova as saying, without elaborating on the nature or origin of the interference.
Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's powerful Security Council who plays an important role in peace talks with Chechnya, said earlier he did not know of the existence of the organisation.

"This whole story is rather surprising," Rybkin said, adding Russia had warned foreign states that their citizens should inform both the federal and local authorities about their presence in Chechnya. The couple had failed to do so, he said.

More than 20 hostages are thought to be being held in Chechnya and another was taken on Sunday, Interfax said. It quoted Chechen police as saying Railkhan Koshkalakov had been abducted by a masked gang who stopped his car.
Major international aid organisations withdrew most of their staff from the region after six Red Cross workers were shot dead in their beds in December by unknown gunmen.
Some foreigners are still working in Grozny for smaller aid organisations, but they keep a low profile.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted the British Foreign Office as saying that it had urged all its citizens to leave Chechnya.

But a Foreign Office spokesman said that while it had long passed on Russia's warning that Moscow could not guarantee foreigners' safety in Chechnya, it had not asked aid workers still there to leave.
